title: Cardiac Dysrhythmias & Conduction Disorders: Rhythm Recognition, Perfusion and Electrical Rescue
html:
A cardiac rhythm is clinically important because of what it does to perfusion, not because the monitor looks unusual. The RN rapidly determines whether the tracing is real, whether the client has a pulse, whether circulation is adequate, what mechanism is likely, and what action cannot wait. Rhythm interpretation, client assessment, and emergency algorithms must remain connected.

Learning goals

  • Analyze rate, regularity, atrial activity, PR interval, and QRS width systematically.
  • Distinguish monitor artifact from a true rhythm and stable from unstable dysrhythmia.
  • Recognize nursing priorities for atrial fibrillation, SVT, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and bradyarrhythmias.
  • Differentiate synchronized cardioversion, defibrillation, and transcutaneous pacing.
  • Identify reversible causes, medication hazards, anticoagulation needs, and postprocedure complications.
  • Evaluate electrical treatment by both rhythm change and restored perfusion.

Assess the client before naming the rhythm

Look for responsiveness, normal breathing, a central pulse, blood pressure, skin signs, mentation, chest discomfort, dyspnea, acute heart failure, syncope, and shock. If the monitor displays a lethal-looking rhythm but the client is talking comfortably, check electrodes, leads, cables, motion, and another lead while continuing assessment. If the client is unresponsive with no normal breathing and no pulse, begin the cardiac-arrest response immediately; do not delay CPR to print a perfect strip.

The monitor is a cue—not the patient
Artifact can resemble ventricular tachycardia or fibrillation, while a dangerous rhythm may produce a deceptively modest rate. Confirm the client, pulse, perfusion, and lead quality without delaying rescue.

Use the same rhythm-analysis sequence every time

  1. Rate: Estimate atrial and ventricular rates and note whether they are expected for the clinical situation.
  2. Regularity: Compare R–R and P–P intervals. Decide whether the rhythm is regular, regularly irregular, or irregularly irregular.
  3. P waves: Determine whether atrial activity is present, uniform, and related to each QRS.
  4. PR interval: Measure whether atrioventricular conduction is consistent and within the expected range.
  5. QRS: Determine whether ventricular depolarization is narrow or wide and whether morphology is uniform.
  6. Context: Integrate symptoms, pulse, pressure, perfusion, prior ECG, medications, electrolytes, oxygenation, ischemia, and structural disease.

A bedside monitor is designed for surveillance and may distort ST segments or rhythm morphology. Obtain a diagnostic 12-lead ECG when indicated. Record the rhythm strip before treatment when this does not delay urgent intervention, and document the client response rather than only the rhythm label.

Instability changes the treatment pathway

Signs that a tachyarrhythmia or bradyarrhythmia is causing cardiopulmonary compromise include hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischemic chest discomfort, acute heart failure, syncope, or other evidence of inadequate perfusion. Establish whether these findings are caused by the rhythm rather than simply occurring alongside it, but do not postpone treatment when the link is clear.

Support airway and breathing, give oxygen when hypoxemic, attach continuous monitoring and defibrillation/pacing pads, obtain IV or intraosseous access as appropriate, acquire a 12-lead ECG if time permits, and call for expert or emergency support. Search simultaneously for reversible causes such as ischemia, hypoxemia, electrolyte disturbance, acid–base disorder, drug toxicity, infection, hemorrhage, hypovolemia, pulmonary embolism, or thyroid disease.

Sinus rhythms can be appropriate or pathologic

Sinus tachycardia is often a physiologic response to pain, fever, hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxemia, anxiety, infection, or other stress. Treat the cause rather than suppressing a compensatory rate reflexively. Sinus bradycardia may be normal during sleep or in trained athletes, but ischemia, hypoxia, hypothermia, medications, increased vagal tone, or conduction disease can make it dangerous.

A rate alone does not define instability. A client with a slow rate and normal mentation, pressure, and perfusion may need observation and cause evaluation, while a client at the same rate with shock or acute heart failure needs immediate support.

Atrial fibrillation creates rate and stroke questions

Atrial fibrillation commonly produces no consistent P waves and an irregularly irregular ventricular response. Symptoms range from none to palpitations, fatigue, dyspnea, dizziness, chest discomfort, heart failure, or shock. Determine onset or last-known normal rhythm when possible, evaluate rate and stability, and assess precipitating conditions.

An unstable client whose compromise is caused by AF may require immediate synchronized cardioversion. Stable management may emphasize rate control, rhythm control, or both based on symptoms, duration, structural disease, comorbidities, and shared decisions. Cardioversion planning must consider atrial thrombus and embolic risk when duration is prolonged or uncertain.

Stroke prevention is separate from rate control. The team estimates annual thromboembolic risk using a validated approach and balances it against bleeding risk, client preferences, valve disease, kidney and liver function, interactions, adherence, and procedural plans. Aspirin is not an equivalent substitute for indicated oral anticoagulation. New weakness, facial droop, speech change, vision loss, or severe imbalance requires immediate stroke evaluation.

Regular narrow-complex tachycardia

A regular narrow-complex tachycardia may represent a reentrant supraventricular tachycardia. Confirm stability and obtain a 12-lead tracing when possible. For a stable regular rhythm, a coached vagal maneuver may be attempted under the current algorithm. Carotid sinus massage is not a routine nursing maneuver and can cause harm in susceptible clients.

Protocol-directed adenosine may be used for selected regular rhythms. Give it through appropriate access with the rapid administration method required by protocol and continuous ECG recording. Warn the alert client that transient flushing, chest pressure, or a brief sense of impending doom can occur. Have resuscitation capability available. Adenosine does not treat atrial fibrillation and should not be used indiscriminately for irregular or polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia.

Wide-complex tachycardia demands caution

Treat an undifferentiated regular wide-complex tachycardia as ventricular tachycardia until expert evaluation establishes otherwise. A client with a pulse and rhythm-caused instability generally needs prompt synchronized cardioversion. A stable client allows time for a 12-lead ECG, expert consultation, and algorithm-directed medication. Avoid AV-nodal blockers that can worsen an unknown ventricular or pre-excited rhythm.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia cannot be reliably synchronized and is treated with an immediate unsynchronized shock when sustained. Torsades de pointes is polymorphic VT associated with prolonged QT; correct causes, stop QT-prolonging contributors, replace deficient electrolytes, and prepare protocol-directed magnesium and electrical therapy.

Pulse determines the ventricular-arrest pathway

Pulseless ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation are shockable cardiac-arrest rhythms. Begin high-quality CPR, attach the defibrillator, deliver unsynchronized shock according to the current algorithm, resume CPR immediately, give algorithm-directed medications, and treat reversible causes. Minimize interruptions and avoid pausing compressions for repeated pulse checks without an organized rhythm.

Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are not shockable. Provide CPR, epinephrine according to the current algorithm, and aggressive evaluation of reversible causes. Verify apparent asystole in more than one lead and check connections without delaying resuscitation.

Synchronized cardioversion and defibrillation are different

Synchronized cardioversion times energy delivery to the R wave to reduce the risk of producing ventricular fibrillation during a vulnerable repolarization period. It is used for selected unstable tachyarrhythmias with a pulse. Confirm that synchronization markers track each QRS, ensure the correct mode and energy, clear the client and bed, and reassess rhythm and perfusion after every shock. If the client is conscious and time permits, provide ordered sedation without delaying lifesaving treatment.

Defibrillation is an unsynchronized shock used for ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and sustained polymorphic VT when synchronization is unreliable. Ensure no one is touching the client, bed, or connected equipment at discharge; manage oxygen and combustible risk according to policy; and resume CPR immediately after a cardiac-arrest shock.

Recheck sync before every cardioversion shock
Some defibrillators leave synchronized mode after a shock. Confirm the markers and mode again before another synchronized shock.

Bradycardia and AV block: treat poor perfusion

Symptomatic bradycardia may cause hypotension, altered mentation, shock, ischemic discomfort, acute heart failure, dizziness, or syncope. Support ABCs, monitor continuously, obtain a 12-lead ECG, evaluate causes, and give protocol-directed atropine when appropriate. If atropine is ineffective or unlikely to work in a high-grade block, prepare transcutaneous pacing and/or an ordered epinephrine or dopamine infusion while arranging expert care and possible transvenous pacing.

First-degree AV block prolongs the PR interval but conducts every atrial impulse. Mobitz I second-degree block progressively lengthens PR intervals before a dropped QRS; it may be transient and less dangerous depending on context. Mobitz II unexpectedly drops QRS complexes without progressive PR lengthening and can advance to complete heart block. Third-degree block has atrial and ventricular activity without a consistent relationship. New Mobitz II or complete block, especially with poor perfusion, requires pacing readiness and urgent escalation.

Transcutaneous pacing requires electrical and mechanical capture

Apply pacing pads in the recommended position, select the prescribed rate, and increase current until electrical capture occurs, then confirm mechanical capture with a palpable pulse and pressure waveform matching each paced complex. Monitor perfusion continuously. Skeletal muscle movement alone does not prove cardiac output.

Conscious pacing can be painful; provide ordered analgesia or sedation when feasible without compromising airway or delaying emergency treatment. Continue to treat the underlying cause and prepare for transvenous pacing if instability persists.

Permanent pacemakers and ICDs

After implantation, monitor rhythm, incision, bleeding, infection, pain, and complications such as pneumothorax, lead displacement, perforation, or tamponade. Follow procedure-specific arm and activity instructions rather than a universal restriction. Pacemaker failure to pace shows absent expected spikes; failure to capture shows a spike without the expected depolarization; failure to sense causes inappropriate pacing. Assess the client first and escalate instability.

An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator shock may be appropriate therapy for a malignant rhythm. One shock with rapid recovery still requires the device team's follow-up plan. Repeated shocks, persistent symptoms, syncope, chest discomfort, dyspnea, or instability require emergency services. Magnets can change device behavior and should be used only under qualified direction and policy.

Medication and electrolyte surveillance prevents recurrence

Review beta blockers, calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, antiarrhythmics, stimulants, decongestants, QT-prolonging drugs, and possible toxins. Trend potassium, magnesium, calcium, kidney and liver function, oxygenation, acid–base status, and drug-specific monitoring. Correcting the rhythm without correcting the cause invites recurrence.

Antiarrhythmic drugs can themselves cause bradycardia, hypotension, conduction block, QT prolongation, or new dysrhythmia. Verify dose, infusion rate, compatibility, access, and monitoring. For anticoagulants, assess bleeding, interactions, renal function, procedures, adherence, and stroke symptoms; never independently stop therapy because the rhythm appears normal.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Assess responsiveness, breathing, pulse, pressure, perfusion, symptoms, rhythm rate and pattern, P waves, PR, QRS, medications, electrolytes, oxygenation, and recent events.
  2. Analyze cues: Verify artifact, identify the likely rhythm mechanism, connect it to the client's condition, and distinguish stable from rhythm-caused compromise.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Pulseless VT/VF, unstable tachycardia, unstable high-grade block, ischemia, severe electrolyte disturbance, and embolic stroke risk outrank precise naming of every waveform.
  4. Generate solutions: Support ABCs, activate help, prepare appropriate electrical therapy, obtain ECG and access, treat reversible causes, and reduce medication and thromboembolic harm.
  5. Take action: Start CPR for pulseless arrest, synchronize shocks for selected unstable tachycardia with a pulse, defibrillate shockable arrest or sustained polymorphic VT, and pace refractory unstable bradycardia as directed.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm pulse, pressure, mentation, symptoms, oxygenation, rhythm, electrical and mechanical capture, adverse effects, and correction of the underlying cause.

Clinical example

A client becomes pale, confused, and hypotensive with a regular wide-complex rhythm at 180/min and a palpable pulse. The RN calls emergency support, applies defibrillation pads, supports ABCs, obtains access, and identifies that the rhythm is causing instability. The team prepares immediate synchronized cardioversion, confirms sync markers on each QRS, provides sedation only if it will not delay treatment, clears the client, and delivers the ordered shock. The RN then reassesses pulse, pressure, mentation, rhythm, oxygenation, and reversible causes instead of declaring success from the monitor alone.

Rhythm diagnosis, ECG interpretation, medication selection and dosing, energy settings, cardioversion, defibrillation, pacing, anticoagulation, and emergency treatment require current algorithms, device instructions, authorized orders, local protocols, expert input, and qualified supervision.
